projects.title: From conference demo to 0→1 source grounded AI workspace
projects.description: Enterprise generative AI and RAG for 150,000+ employees
projects.case_study_content:
# Overview Confidential work. Product names, UI details, and proprietary metrics are generalized. I designed a conference demo for a senior leader to show customers what generative AI could do on internal knowledge. It became the sanctioned workspace where the company tested models, generation, and RAG on real business workflows. The intended destination for employees was always multi-turn chat in search. That is where employees already look for company knowledge. The workspace existed because that change was not ready. People still trusted search over conversation, and accuracy was too weak to risk adding multi-turn search at the current stage. The workspace had 2 modes: Generate and Q&A. The workspace shipped to 150,000+ employees and became the primary tool teams used for basic generation, to building internal agent experiences. The conversational workspace later went offline when a third-party partnership became the path forward for both generation and business workflows. The quality bar, retrieval strategy, and the UX guardrails remain. The partner API is what will put multi-turn conversation back into search once testing domain specific assistants is complete. # The challenge **The original brief was a demo.** Once this became a workspace, enterprise search was still a link list. People typed jobs and policies (“how do I…”, “what is the policy for…”). Prior AI pilots had already taught them not to trust fluent answers with no sources, no permissions, and no recovery when the model was wrong. **Early retrieval ran 30–45 seconds.** A spinner was a dead end. Early RAG could attach only three documents per turn. Against a large unscoped source pool, the model could not choose well. **Shadow AI was already in use.** The company needed one sanctioned place for employees to learn what LLMs were for, and a quality bar for when (or whether) knowledge answers could return to search. # My role & impact ## Design - Interaction, visual design, and production specs - High-fidelity prototypes that simulated retrieval and conversation months before infrastructure existed. - Design-system patterns: citations, source panels, prompt libraries, attachments, thread states. - Agent UI integration using MCP hooks for live, permissioned data. ## Leadership - Turned a senior-leader demo request into a funded project. - Secured executive backing inside the company. - Product design strategy for employee-experience AI: what to sanction, what to keep out of search, what to retire. - Led 2 designers, 6 engineers, and multiple stakeholders. ## Research - 1:1 interviews, surveys, and unmoderated tests (UserZoom, dScout) across NA, EMEA, APAC, LATAM. - LLM-assisted synthesis to turn qualitative data into use cases and a quality bar. - Model benchmarking on internal knowledge tasks for accuracy, not just fluency. # Alignment workshops Facilitated a **2-day** diverge/converge and battleship prioritization workshop with **15 participants** from Engineering, Product, and HR. * **73 ideas** generated against a "How might we" challenge for AI-assisted search * **13 priorities** ranked by user value and level of effort * Output: research-backed product backlog aligned across org boundaries # Research insights ## Task-driven work, not keywords Employees needed jobs done and policies followed. A demo can show possibility. A workspace has to match intent. ## Trust favored sourced answers over chat For specialized internal knowledge, people trusted what they could verify. Fluent answers with no sources were treated as the last failed pilot. Non-deterministic wording still read as risk, and as a reason to keep multi-turn conversation out of search. ## Collections had to be scoped by audience Legal, HR, and Sales could not share one open corpus. A three-document cap only works if the pool is already the right pool. Permissions belonged in the answer, not only in the backend. # Key decisions ## Hold it out of search until quality is good enough - Search was the destination for knowledge answers. - Early answers were not reliable enough to sit next to directory results. - After the demo, we kept Generate and Q&A in a workspace so the company could test and evolve use cases without poisoning search.
Tradeoff: A second surface, on purpose. Search kept sourced answers. Conversation lived in the workspace until it earned a place next to results. On this product, that conversational piece moved to a 3rd party. We may bring that API back into search now that it holds. ## Split Generate from Search / Q&A - Early models could not reliably do grounded Q&A and open generation in one surface on company knowledge. We shipped two jobs: Search / Q&A for cited answers, Generate for drafts and summarization.
Tradeoff: Two modes to learn, and a cleaner trust model. Employees always knew which job they were in. ## Scope the retrieval, then accept the remaining risk - Early RAG pulled three documents per turn from a large unscoped pool. - The model could not choose well. Knowledge collections scoped each search. Answers got better, still inconsistent. - An MCP server made retrieval reliable enough to depend on. The answers were still non-deterministic.
That residual distrust is why citations, permissions, and separate jobs stayed in the product, why conversation stayed off search, and why a later HR surface needed its own eval bar.
Tradeoff: Better retrieval does not equal a trusted sentence. We designed for that gap instead of waiting for the model to become deterministic. ## Citation-first answers - Source visibility and permission-scoped citations over fluent chat prose.
Tradeoff: Denser responses. Higher trust after pilots that had felt like magic. Still not enough to put conversation next to directory results. # The solution This started as a conference demo for a senior leader. It became a dual-mode workspace: Generate for drafts and summarization, Q&A for cited answers. **Phase 1 (2023–2024)** · First integration We put a generative panel in the existing portal. - The first version read like a banner ad and sat too wide. - The second stripped the graphics so we could see if the interaction itself worked. - The third added “ask a follow-up” so a result could become a thread. That was enough to learn from. Quality did not hold, and Generate did not fit a results panel. **Phase 2 (2024–2026)** · AI Workspace This is the product in the galleries. Prompt library, attachments, cited answers, two modes. - Early RAG could only pull three documents from a large unscoped pool, so the model often picked poorly. - Knowledge collections narrowed each query. Answers got better, still inconsistent. - MCP made retrieval reliable enough to depend on. The wording stayed non-deterministic, which is why we kept citations and kept the two jobs separate. It shipped. People used it. **What happened next** Model quality stalled. A large 3rd party partnership became the path forward. The conversational workspace went offline. AI answers in search stayed. Use cases, citations, prompt library, dual modes, and permissioned collections moved into domain-specific knowledge assistants.

impact.title: Impact
impact.content:
**0→1:** Conference demo to a shipped dual-mode workspace. No prior sanctioned generative or RAG surface.

**Shipped:** Used by 150,000+ employees.

**Retrieval:** Knowledge collections plus RAG and MCP improved retrieval by 35%.

**Latency:** Progressive status for 30–45 second retrieval, not a spinner.

**Sunset:** 
- The conversational workspace went offline when a 3rd party partnership became the path forward. 
- AI answers in search stayed. 
- Learnings, and later the partner API, are what can return conversation to search.

**Reuse:** Citations, prompt library, dual modes, and permissioned collections moved into domain-specific assistants.

projects.title: Music experience platform
projects.description: Poster art becomes the virtual stage.
projects.case_study_content:
# Overview
I play guitar in flACID and I own brand and product.

Fans, the band, and venues needed one product: listen, publish, and live visualizations. Most band sites treat those as separate features.

I designed and built one platform with a single playback engine, interaction language, and design system (Cosmic Signal) in production code.
# My role & impact
## Leadership and strategy
- Framed the product as three audiences, one system: fans, band admins, venues.
- Defined experience modes (Browse, Hero stage, Descent, Stage) with explicit chrome and z-index rules.
- Set the quality bar for AI-assisted production: automation for scale, human judgment for IA and taste.
- Documented decisions with rejected alternatives.
## Design and systems
- End-to-end IA, visual identity, interaction roles, and responsive behavior.
- Cosmic Signal design system: semantic tokens to brand classes to live specimens.
- Hero-first playback: opt-in stage, in-place catalog play, mutually exclusive transport chrome.
- Legibility system for custom illustration: scrims, dock placement, reserved gradient moments.
## Build and delivery
- Shipped a production React app with Supabase CMS, Web Audio analyser, 20 viz modes, and Stage projection.
- Performance: lazy sections, WebP hero, analyser pause off-screen, mobile and desktop.



# The challenge
Most band sites split listening, publishing, and performance. Fans experience them as one session: browse while a track plays, jump back to the hero, then see the same visuals at a show.

The real constraint was the art. Poster art started as a static canvas. EQ-reactive vizuals and custom illustration turned it into the listening stage. The UI cannot compete with the art. It has to stay legible and rare.

How do you unify fan playback, band content operations, and projected visuals in one product, with an interaction language a team could build upon?














# Research insights
## Differentiation is experiential
Streaming already plays the tracks. The site has to offer mixed media, reactive visuals, and editorial depth that a player app does not.
## Legibility on illustration is non-negotiable
Custom hero and album art carry the brand. Player, nav, and type have to work on top of that art without covering baked-in typography.
## One player surface at a time
When the hero dock and the header mini player both appear, users lose orientation on a reactive canvas. Mutually exclusive player chrome became a product rule enforced in logic, not styling alone.



# Key decisions
## Hero-first playback
**Chosen:** The hero is the primary listening surface: poster when idle, full visualizer when playing. Discography plays in place. Only explicit Listen now and the viz showcase scroll to the stage.

**Rejected:** A dedicated Listen Now section that hijacked scroll on every track tap.

**Why:** Fans browse discography while listening. Forced scroll feels like a demo, not a product. Hero-stage is opt-in. The header mini player keeps control when they scroll away.

## Three interaction roles
**Chosen:** Primary fill for CTAs (Play, tickets). Neon green for nav-active (tabs, section nav, Descend on). Purple-bright for control rest, green on hover.

**Rejected:** Gradient CTAs everywhere, and cyan/fuchsia template accents on every surface.

**Why:** One scan path on a busy psychedelic canvas. Gradients reserved for the Gallery title and footer wordmark so emphasis stays rare.
## Four experience modes, one product

**Chosen:** Browse, Hero stage, Descent (desktop overlay), and Stage (/stage for venues), what shows, and in what order.

**Rejected:** Treating fullscreen player, Descent, and Stage as unrelated features bolted onto a band template.

**Why:** Same audio engine, different surfaces, documented in the design system so design and engineering share one model.

## Cosmic Signal identity
**Chosen:** Void base, hot-pink section titles, green eyebrows, custom hero and album art. Syne display, Instrument Sans body.

**Rejected:** Generic synthwave gradient on every heading. Stock photography under a strong custom hero.

**Why:** Art leads the brand. UI supports legibility on illustration: logo scrim, chest dock, no cover overlay on baked-in album type.
# The solution
An immersive, visual-forward band site. The hero is the stage for live reactive visualizations. One audio engine, four modes: Hero, catalog, Descent, and Stage.

The band publishes through the Cosmic Signal design system, not a template site.

# Key features
## Band CMS
Sign-in unlocks edit mode. The band updates tour, gallery, tracks, and copy without a developer: inline sections, media upload, section visibility, and draft to publish.
## Stage projection
`/stage` broadcasts reactive visualizations from live audio. Control stays on one surface. Projection is a second window.
## Visualization catalog
20 EQ-reactive modes plus a WebGL tunnel, tied to the gallery and the hero stage.
## One listening session
Hero dock and header mini player never show together. Catalog plays in place. One engine across Browse, Hero, Descent, and Stage.


# Results
Shipped in 3 months, solo. Live immersive site for fans, the band, and Stage. The band publishes without a developer.

projects.case_study_content: # Overview I designed, built, and deployed a custom portfolio platform to replace the limitations of Squarespace, creating a scalable, AI-assisted CMS for publishing and managing projects. The system enables a 5× faster content workflow, full control over SEO and performance, and a flexible architecture for ongoing iteration and feature development. This project was built using an AI-assisted design-to-code workflow, moving from product definition and system design in Figma to rapid implementation using Cursor, Supabase, and Vercel. Live in production and actively used as my primary publishing platform. This project is evolving on a regular basis and is not finished, stay tuned for updates. View the code on GitHub # Key features ## Flexible content management system Leveraged AI-powered workflows to architect a custom Admin UI and Supabase backend, enabling real-time content management decoupled from the codebase. ## High-Performance asset pipeline Implemented Supabase Storage with automated image/video optimization, ensuring sub-second LCP (Largest Contentful Paint). ## Relational data model Architected a relational database schema in Supabase to manage complex project relationships and metadata. ## Scalable design system Developed a reusable React component library with Tailwind CSS, supporting auto-detection of system themes and frictionless UI scaling. ## Dark/Light Theme Auto-detection of system theme; toggle between themes ## Integrated SEO & Meta-Management Built a dedicated SEO console for granular control over social graphing, indexing, and search visibility.

projects.title: Skype for Android + Skype Qik
projects.description: Conversation-first communication at 100M+ users, then a 0→1 rethink of mobile video.
projects.case_study_content:
# Overview
Communication is inherently multimodal ... voice, video, text, files ... but Skype still forced people into rigid modes and synchronous expectations. As Design Lead on Skype for Android, I helped pivot the product toward a conversation-first experience at 100M+ user scale. That work exposed a second problem: even inside a unified thread, video still felt heavy: scheduling, performance, and the awkwardness of "being on."

I then led a Tiger Team for Skype Qik, a 0→1 product that treated video as lightweight, asynchronous conversation rather than a mini TV call. Together, these two chapters show the same through-line: **modalities should emerge from intent, not feel like explicit mode switches.**

# My role & impact

## Leadership

- Design Lead for Skype for Android, owned end-to-end interaction design across multiple major releases at global scale
- Only US-based designer on the mobile team for the first year; scaled the Android design team to 5 (interaction, visual, research)
- Led Skype Qik Tiger Team (7 designers, researchers, and engineers) for a cross-platform 0→1 launch on iOS, Android, and Windows Phone
- Produced comprehensive interaction specs with platform-specific notes for engineering across phone and tablet form factors


## Design & research

- Replaced dashboard IA with conversation-first architecture — unified text, voice, video, and files in a single thread
- Conducted generative research with younger demographics that informed Qik's async, expressive video model
- Designed persistent viewfinder capture, horizontal video timeline, and gesture-first navigation for Qik
- Defined notification, sign-in, and multimodal message-state patterns across Android releases

## Result

- Shipped conversation-first Skype for Android used by 100M+ people
- Delivered Skype's first standalone mobile app beyond the main client (Qik)
- Pioneered the async video conversation pattern later validated by competitors like Marco Polo
- Qik's core interaction model was integrated into the broader Skype ecosystem after sunset




# Research insights
## Conversations over dashboard

Users don't think in product modes, they think in relationships. Replacing hub-and-spoke navigation with conversation-first IA made async features discoverable and turned modality switching into continuing the same dialogue.

## Video should behave like messaging

Even inside a unified thread, video still felt like a scheduled performance. Research and market shifts showed users wanted spontaneous, replayable clips, not another call. That insight justified Qik as a new product model, not "more Skype."

## Spontaneity drives expression

The less effort required to capture and send, the more people share. Persistent camera readiness, gesture-initiated recording, and a horizontal timeline were designed to drive time-to-capture toward zero and keep focus on the conversation.


# Phase 1: Multimodal communication at scale
Skype's mobile experience was fragmented: voice, video, chat, and file sharing lived in separate mental models. Users thought "Skype = video calls," not "my conversations." Weak discoverability and mode-switching friction made async features hard to find and use.

#### What I led

* **Replaced hub-and-spoke navigation** with conversation-first information architecture
* **Unified modalities** inside a single thread so people could move between text, voice, video, and files without re-orienting
* **Shipped across Android 2.5+ through 5.x**, phone and tablet, as the platform evolved from Gingerbread through Lollipop
* **Expanded sign-in flows** (Microsoft account, Skype name, email, phone) to reduce onboarding friction
* **Defined core interactions**, message states, file transfer flows, inline call events, and native notification patterns at spec depth

This phase established the container. Phase 2 rethought the medium where it was still broken.




# Phase 2: Skype Qik — zero-friction video
Even after unifying modalities, video remained synchronous-by-default: it demanded scheduling, attention, and a kind of performance. Meanwhile, Snapchat, Vine, and short-form video apps were training users to expect spontaneous, low-effort, replayable expression.

#### The problem

* **Video calls felt heavy**, awkward, and hard to coordinate
* **Messaging was preferred to calling** by users
* **Async video conversation** with ephemeral, social, or broadcast features were becoming more popular than scheduled calls

#### What I led

* **0→1 interaction model:** phone-number based, native address book, no Skype ID required
* **Zero-friction capture:** persistent viewfinder + gesture-initiated recording
* **Horizontal video timeline:** continuous playback where each clip reads as a scene in a movie — not an endless vertical chat scroll
* **Gesture-first navigation:** interaction over chrome — flick down to record, flick up for recent conversations
* **Cross-platform** release spec covering Android, iOS, and Windows Phone from a single design source



# Competitive analysis
## Snapchat

Context: Fun, disappearing messages that appealed to a younger demographic.

Gap: The ephemeral nature limited deeper, ongoing group conversations.

Qik Advantage: Provided a persistent, high-quality "movie" of the conversation while keeping the capture just as fast.

## Vine

Context: Dominated the "short-form creative" space with 6-second loops.

Gap: Not designed for 1-1 or group back-and-forth communication.

Qik Advantage: Focused on the conversation, not the broadcast, using the same "snackable" video format.

## Periscope / Meerkat

Context: Focused on live broadcasting and "in-the-moment" streaming.

Gap: Required synchronous presence; if you weren't there live, you missed it.

Qik Advantage: Mastered asynchronicity, allowing users to contribute to the "video thread" whenever they were ready.
# Key features
### Zero-friction recording

Persistent viewfinder and swipe-down gesture put the camera one motion away from capture, no feed, no clutter, no mode picker.

### Horizontal video timeline

Tested vertical chat vs. horizontal timeline; the cinematic sequence model won, fewer transitions, more focus on content, conversations that read like playback-through-dialogue.

### Lightweight UI

Stripped social-feed patterns and persistent chrome. The UI stays out of the way so human connection stays in focus, a principle that still guides how I think about multimodal AI interfaces today.

---

# Key takeaways
- Skype for Android proved that multimodal communication works when modalities live inside a conversation container, not a settings panel. 
- Skype Qik proved that video can be as spontaneous and effortless as texting when you redesign the medium, not just the feature set.

Together, these projects show a progression: from structured modality switching to fluid, expressive interaction, where intent leads and the interface gets out of the way.

projects.title: MassRoots for iOS and Android
projects.description: Turning a failing social network into a cannabis discovery platform, with compliance and a B2B marketplace.
projects.case_study_content:
# Overview MassRoots, a social network for cannabis enthusiasts, was losing users and revenue. The app had a confusing experience, poor ratings (iOS 3.3, Android 2.9), and no monetization model. Competitors (Leafly, Weedmaps) were pulling ahead. The mission was to transform MassRoots from a struggling social network into a community-driven discovery platform that connected consumers with products, reviews, and dispensaries. # My role ## Leadership * **Defined UX strategy** across consumer + B2B experiences * **Established design system** for consistency across platforms * **Created user research framework** for ongoing feedback loops * **Integrated design** into the product and engineering workflow * **Introduced dual-track agile** to align discovery with delivery * **Built and led** 3–4 designer team * **Defined career ladder** → ensured growth and retention * **Collaborated with execs** and sales to shape roadmap + GTM ## Design - Designed end-to-end user experience for content discovery - Created a comprehensive design system for consistency - Prototyped and tested new features continuously with real users - Built and shipped features that increased engagement by 300% ## Research - Conducted user research studies with 50+ cannabis users - Analyzed data and insights to understand user behavior - Validated design decisions through A/B testing - Tested prototypes with users to ensure usability # Research insights ## From Social to Utility Research shifted our north star from "Content Consumption" to "Product Discovery"—solving for the user's true intent: What is good, and where is it? ## Native-First Capture Discovered in-app camera friction; deprioritized custom filters in favor of native OS hooks to align with established user behavior. ## Brand De-stigmatization Identified a critical rejection of "Stoner" tropes; pivoted the design system toward a professional, clinical-meets-lifestyle aesthetic to drive inclusivity. # Competitive analysis ## Leafly Cannabis information and strain rating app • No ability to rate products • Strain ratings highly variable based on producer • Limited social component ## Weedmaps Cannabis dispensary locater • Dispensary ratings • No products ratings • No social component ## Vivino Wine ratings and reviews • Individual wine ratings • Wine maker ratings • Social component ## Rex Recommends places to visit • Ratings for restaurants, parks, stores, etc. • No ratings for products • Product with limited social component # The solution Armed with these insights, we rallied around a new vision: to become the go-to cannabis discovery engine. This meant a complete overhaul of the app's core functionality. # Registration, onboarding and compliance We streamlined the sign-up process, guiding new users to content that was immediately relevant to their location and interests. One important business problem we had to solve as a publicly traded company, was how might we serve people in legal cannabis markets without stepping out of compliance with recreational and medical marijuana legislation being passed at the state level? • Simplified sign-up flow with geo-fencing for legal states only • Dropped-off users reduced, compliance maintained • Onboarding experience served as education for users # Product reviews Our key differentiator was integrating a powerful review system. Users could now share detailed product reviews, complete with their ratings and experiences. This created a new layer of trust and authenticity. • Introduced 5-star review system (avoided weed-leaf icons) • Supported tagging, product attributes, and dispensary linkage • Standardized product descriptions (taste, smell, effects) # Navigation, feeds, and business profiles We redesigned the main navigation to prioritize the most important features: local discovery, social feeds, and product reviews. Since we were adding cannabis reviews to the platform, we wanted them to have visibility in the network. To address this we added a new feed that only focused on cannabis reviews. • Redesigned nav to prioritize Discovery, Reviews, Local • Following** feed (opt-in social) • Reviews** feed (product info & ratings) • Local** feed (nearby users & businesses) • Global** feed (community-wide) • Enhanced business profile design # Dispensary finder The dispensary finder was a solution to provide consumers access to the best products at local businesses, while also providing important consumer information about preferences and trends. We built a robust local dispensary finder, complete with business profiles, menus, and user reviews. This not only served our users but also opened up a new revenue stream for the business. **Phase 1** • Geo-located dispensaries with color-coded medical vs recreational pins • Business profiles with menus, reviews, and social feeds • Monetization via premium placements, ads
**Phase 2** • Online ordering • Rewards system • Subscriptions # Search, explore, and strain pages The Explore experience needed to help us promote the dispensary finder, which was a new revenue stream for the company. • Browse trending posts, search across users, hashtags, strains • Strain/product pages tied to local dispensary listings • Prominent location for the dispensary finder within Explore • Positioned as the "Vivino for cannabis"

projects.title: Tandem Diabetes Care
projects.description: First touchscreen insulin pump. FDA-cleared, 65% fewer use errors, 27% faster training.
projects.case_study_content:
# Overview

As the first product designer at Tandem, I defined the UX and design strategy for the t:slim insulin pump, the first touchscreen insulin pump on the market. This FDA-cleared, award-winning device redefined design and usability in the diabetes tech industry and became Tandem’s flagship product, helping propel the company from startup to IPO.

**Mission**
* Deliver the industry’s first consumer-grade insulin pump interface
* Create a product that patients trust, understand, and want to use
* Reduce use errors while increasing training efficiency for clinicians
* Establish a design-driven culture inside a highly regulated, engineering-led organization

# My role & impact

## Leadership
* Hired and led Tandem’s first internal design team.
* Championed design strategy with executives, the FDA, and clinical stakeholders.
* Integrated UX into the Scrum process, bridging the gap between clinical research and hardware engineering.

## Design
• Executed end-to-end UX, building frameworks and interaction models from scratch.
* Created reusable UI patterns specifically for a high-contrast, medical-grade touchscreen.
* Designed the "Bolus Calculator" and safety-confirmation logic to prevent accidental delivery.

## Research
* Conducted ethnographic studies with 40+ patients, nurses, and endocrinologists.
* Led task-based usability tests to validate safety-critical workflows.
* Synthesized research into a "Trust-First" design language that addressed user intimidation.
# The challenge
**Awareness:** 
Patients often struggle to understand all the complex inputs required for calculating insulin delivery.

**Metabolic Feedback:** 
Current pumps fail to give adequate feedback on how insulin is metabolized, leading to potential stacking and hypoglycemic events.

**Stigma & Aesthetics:** 
Market research revealed that "medical-looking" devices made patients self-conscious. There was a desperate need for a device that looked like consumer tech, not a pager.

**Physical Constraints:** 
Designing for compromised finger dexterity, vision impairment, and emergency hypoglycemic states where cognitive function is lowered.
# Research insights

## Look and feel importance
Patients are already self-conscious about their disease, so they do not want to call more attention to themselves.

## Awareness
People don’t understand all of the inputs for calculating their own insulin delivery.

## How insulin is metabolized affects potential outcomes
People don't understand insulin on board and how it is metabolized because current pumps do not give them good enough feedback or education during use.

## Existing solutions are difficult to use
Navigation is cumbersome and information is not organized in an intuitive way.

## Intimidating language
Alerts and alarms tended to be scary and intimidating, without help for resolving the issue.

# Competitive analysis
## Animas One Touch Ping

Strength: Strong continuous glucose monitoring but complex interface.

Highlight: Excellent glucose data accuracy.

## Medtronic Paradigm

Strength: Good integration with pumps but outdated design.

Highlight: Strong pump integration.

## Omnipod

Defining Feature: The defining feature is the tubeless design.

Highlight: Automatic cannula insertion.

# The solution: A new direction
I redesigned the Tandem app to focus on simplicity and patient empowerment. The new design focused on meeting patients where they are and not allowing their lifestyle to be impacted by their insulin therapy.
# Key features

## Insulin onboard indicator

This allowed patients to understand how much insulin is in their system based on their most recent meal, considering their blood glucose level, insulin to carb ratio, and current basal rate.

## Touch screen keypad 

Allows direct manipulation and entry of values for blood glucose, bolus calculations, and settings like the insulin to carb ratio. Competitor products required scrolling through a list of values before selecting one

## Extended bolus

Allowed a bolus to be delivered over a period of time to account for situations like snacking over a long period vs dedicated meals.

## Quick bolus

Allowed a bolus to be delivered without looking at the screen based on gestures using a single hardware button.

## Personal profiles

Allowed patients to fully customize their insulin settings for different situations, such as high / low energy activities, work, sickness, etc.

---

---

writingPosts.title: You shipped a pilot and called it GA
writingPosts.subtitle: AI Agent Behavior Design
writingPosts.excerpt: Most "AI agents" in production are just undocumented workflows with confidence.

blocks.text: Most "AI agents" in production are just undocumented workflows with confidence.

blocks.content:
I've reviewed enough agent work to know the demo is never the problem. The problem is everything the demo doesn't show. 

When I sit down to review one, I'm really asking three questions. If the team can't answer them, the agent isn't ready, no matter how good the happy path looks.

1. What is this agent not allowed to do?

2. What does the user see when the answer is uncertain?

3. What does the user see when something fails?

### 1. What is this agent not allowed to do? Most agents are specified by what they can do. The boundaries are left implicit, which means the model decides them live, under pressure, in front of a user. - "Answer billing questions" is a capability. - "Never quote a refund amount, never promise a date, escalate anything involving a dispute" is a boundary. If the team can only list capabilities, the agent will discover its own limits in production, and usually in the worst possible case. A good solution here reads like a short list of hard "no" rules.

### 2. What does the user see when the answer is uncertain?
Confidence is a design decision, not a model property. The failure I see most often is an agent that sounds exactly as sure when retrieval was strong as when it was thin. The user has no way to tell a solid answer from a guess, so they trust both, and get burned by the guess. Designing for uncertainty means deciding what changes in the interface when the system isn't sure: hedged language, a visible source, a "want me to double-check?" prompt, or simply declining. If nothing in the product changes when confidence drops, that's the bug.

### 3. What does the user see when something fails?
Teams invest in the failure they can see: logging, alerts, dashboards. That's the team's experience of failure. **The user's experience is usually undesigned.** A tool times out and the user gets a spinner, or a cheerful confirmation for something that didn't happen.

blocks.text: If the answer to "what does the user see" lives in Slack or Confluence, it isn't designed yet.

blocks.content:
A real answer describes what the person on the other end sees and can do next:

- a clear message
- a way to recover
- a path to a human with context.

blocks.text:
If those three questions aren't answered before launch, you didn't ship an agent.

You shipped a pilot and called it GA.

writingPosts.title: What if the happy path is a dead end...?
writingPosts.subtitle: AI Agent Behavior Design
writingPosts.excerpt: We made it trivial to deploy agents. We did not make it trivial to decide what they're allowed to do.

blocks.text: We made it trivial to deploy agents. We did not make it trivial to decide what they're allowed to do.

blocks.content:
I work on enterprise AI today. Before that I worked in consumer at global scale and in FDA-regulated medical devices, where you don't get to "figure it out in production".

Agents don't get that discipline. Deploy is cheap now, so teams skip behavior design and run this playbook instead:

• Pick a framework 
• Wire up tools 
• Demo the happy path 
• Ship to a pilot 
• Fix what breaks when real users show up

blocks.text: That's not strategy...that's YOLO with a staging environment.

blocks.content:
Screens get designed. Prompts get iterated. But the actual behavior (permissions, refusals, escalation, failure paths, what happens when the model is wrong) too often gets "figured out in prod."

Easy deploy is a massive competitive advantage. But it’s a liability when 'behavior design' is treated as an afterthought instead of a prerequisite.

#### Here's what each of those means when you actually sit down to design it:

- **Permissions:** what the agent can do on its own, and what needs a human to approve first
- **Refusals:** what it should never do, and how it declines without sounding broken
- **Escalation and handoff:** what the user sees while they wait, and whether the human gets enough context to help
- **Failure paths:** what happens when a tool times out or the model is wrong. Retry, fall back, refuse, or escalate

blocks.text: None of that shows up in a demo. All of it shows up in production.

blocks.content:
#### Here's the version I keep seeing. 
- An agent gets asked to do something it **isn't authorized to do**. 
- Nobody designed a refusal, so it produces a confident, plausible response that implies the action happened. 
- It didn't. 
- The user believes it did. Now it's a trust problem and a support ticket, instead of a design decision that cost an hour upfront.

blocks.text: The model wasn't wrong. The edge cases were never designed. Only the happy path was.
